title: How Google Ads Works
subtitle: The auction and Quality Score in plain English
youtube_title: How Google Ads Works: The Auction and Quality Score | Google Ads Course Lesson 1
description: Lesson 1 of the free Google Ads course. Before you launch a campaign, understand how Google decides which ads show and how much you pay. In this lesson: the search ad auction, Ad Rank, Quality Score and its three parts, why the highest bid does not always win, and how your actual cost per click is calculated.

slides.narration: Hi, I'm Khalil Baghirov, and welcome to lesson one of this free Google Ads course. Today we answer the most important question before you spend any money: when someone searches on Google, how does Google decide which ads appear, in what order, and how much each advertiser pays?

Here's the core idea. Every time someone types a search on Google, an auction happens in the background. Google looks at every advertiser who wants to show an ad for that search, and in a fraction of a second, decides which ads are eligible and in what order they appear.

slides.title: What decides your position: Ad Rank
items: The quality of your ad and landing page
The search context: device, location, time
Your ad assets, like sitelinks and calls
slides.narration: Your position is decided by something called Ad Rank. Ad Rank depends on a few things. Your maximum bid. The quality of your ad and your landing page. The context of the search, like the device, location, and time of day. And the expected impact of your ad assets, like sitelinks and call buttons.

slides.title: The three parts of Quality Score
slides.narration: Google summarizes quality with Quality Score, rated from one to ten for each keyword. It has three parts. First, expected click-through rate: how likely people are to click your ad. Second, ad relevance: how closely your ad matches what the person searched. And third, landing page experience: whether your page is useful, fast, and relevant to the ad.

slides.title: Higher bid vs higher quality
bad: Pays more for a lower position
slides.narration: This is why the highest bid does not always win. An advertiser with a big bid but a generic ad and a slow landing page can lose to an advertiser with a fair bid and a highly relevant ad. Google wants searchers to be happy, so it rewards quality with better positions and lower costs.

slides.title: What you actually pay
slides.formula: You pay just enough to beat the Ad Rank below you
slides.note: Your *max bid* is a ceiling, not the price
slides.narration: And here's the good news about cost. You usually don't pay your maximum bid. In the classic auction model, you pay just enough to beat the Ad Rank of the advertiser below you. Your maximum bid is a ceiling, not the price. Better quality means you need less money to hold the same position.

slides.title: What this means for you
items: Write ads that repeat the searcher's words
Send each ad to a matching landing page
Watch Quality Score for every keyword
slides.narration: Here is what this means in practice. One: group your keywords tightly by topic. Two: write ads that use the same words the person searched. Three: send each ad to a landing page that matches it exactly. And four: check the Quality Score of your keywords regularly, and fix the weakest part first.

slides.title: Your homework
items: Search for your own service on Google
Note which ads appear and what they promise
Compare their landing pages with yours
slides.narration: Your homework for today. Search for your own service on Google, the way a customer would. Note which ads appear and what they promise. Then open their landing pages and compare them with yours. You will start seeing the auction through Google's eyes.

slides.next: Setting Up Your Google Ads Account
slides.narration: In the next lesson, we will set up your Google Ads account step by step and avoid the settings that waste money from day one. Subscribe so you don't miss it, and I'll see you in lesson two.
